title: Jeff Goldblum, John Turturro, Rian Johnson and More Set for Marrakech Film Festival Conversations
description: Hollywood stars Jeff Goldblum and John Turturro, and “Knives Out” director Rian Johnson are among those set to take part in the Conversations progr
body:
Hollywood stars Jeff Goldblum and John Turturro, and “Knives Out” director Rian Johnson are among those set to take part in the Conversations program during the 23rd edition of the Marrakech Film Festival, which runs Nov. 20-28.

	Other movieworld luminaries to take part include actress Monica Bellucci, directors James Gray, Luca Guadagnino, Cristian Mungiu, Laïla Marrakchi, Xavier Dolan and Arthur Harari, and actor-director Gilles Lellouche.
	

	The festival commented that the Conversations would “offer a comprehensive overview of the sensibilities that are shaping contemporary cinema. Whether in major Hollywood productions or deeply personal works, genre films or intimate narratives, their experiences reveal a wide range of approaches to depicting the world, examining society and moving audiences.”

	In a separate announcement on Monday, the festival said that it would honor Goldblum, Turturro and Moroccan actor Younès Mégri during the event.

	Goldblum, whose credits range from David Cronenberg’s “The Fly” to Jon M. Chu’s “Wicked,” said, “It is beyond a thrill and a privilege to be honored at the iconic Marrakech International Film Festival. What a captivating place! This glorious city with such deep roots in storytelling and craftsmanship! I feel wildly lucky indeed. It is truly a rapturous joy—and an adventure upon which I can’t wait to embark.”

	Turturro, whose work includes Spike Lee’s “Do the Right Thing” and the Coen brothers’ “The Big Lebowski,” said, “There is something particularly meaningful about having one’s work celebrated in a place with such a rich cultural history and such a deep appreciation for the art of storytelling. Cinema has a remarkable way of bringing us together, opening windows into other worlds and reminding us of our shared humanity.”
	

	Turturro’s recent film “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” will screen at the festival.

	Mégri, who started his career as a singer and composer, said, “I did not leave music for film; I just switched instruments. This tribute in Marrakech tells me that the audience heard the same sincerity in both. That’s what moves me the most.”

	His international work includes “The Miracles of Jesus” by Jean-Claude Bragard, “The Government Inspector” by Peter Kosminsky, “Laila, la pure” by Gabriel Axel, “David” by Robert Markowitz and “Marie de Nazareth” by Jean Delannoy.

schema.headline: Jeff Goldblum, John Turturro, Rian Johnson and More Set for Marrakech Film Festival Conversations

title: China Box Office: ‘Traces of Justice’ Reclaims Top Spot as Local Debuts ‘Embers’ and ‘The Coffin Swap’ Arrive
description: New Classics Pictures’ crime procedural drama “Traces of Justice” rebounded to first place at the mainland China box office during the Nov. 6–8 wee
body:
New Classics Pictures’ crime procedural drama “Traces of Justice” rebounded to first place at the mainland China box office during the Nov. 6–8 weekend, collecting RMB21.5 million ($3.2 million) over the three-day frame, according to data from Artisan Gateway. 

	The performance lifted the multi-decade investigation epic to $103.7 million since its Oct. 1 release. Directed by Chen Sicheng (“Detective Chinatown”) and co-written with Zhang Ji and Yan Zijie, the drama stars Zhang Yi, Ma Li, and Chen Minghao alongside Karry Wang, Fan Chengcheng, and Chen Feiyu in a narrative tracking an elite public security detective solving complex historical cases based on real events.
	

	Constantin Film and Sony Pictures’ horror reboot “Resident Evil” moved to second position after a month-long reign atop the charts, taking in $3 million in its fifth weekend. The video game adaptation has now reached a cumulative haul of $76 million since launching during the Golden Week corridor on Oct. 5. 

	Tencent Penguin Pictures’ road drama “Embers” debuted in third place, grossing $2.1 million across its two-day opening frame following a Saturday, November 7 rollout. Written and directed by Sun Aoqian, the film stars Song Jia as a weary crematorium worker who accidentally mixes up two sets of funeral ashes. When the families refuse to switch them back, she partners with the deceased’s daughter, played by Vicky Chen, on a journey across the country to return the remains. The cast also features Zu Feng.

	Shanghai Captain’s rural black comedy-thriller “The Coffin Swap” opened in fourth position, pulling in $1.7 million over its two-day weekend debut. Directed by He Nian from a script by Chen Lu, the feature re-adapts Xin Yukun’s 2014 mystery classic “Deep in the Heart” through the lens of He’s acclaimed stage production. Starring Jiang Wu, Du Guangyi, Gu Xin, Fan Yilin, and Wang Weishuai, the narrative unfolds in a secluded village thrown into chaotic intrigue and conflicting cover-ups after an unidentified charred body is discovered.
	

	Beijing Joy Fun Pictures’ body-swap comedy “Mr. & Mrs. Pardon” rounded out the top five, adding $1.4 million in its sixth weekend to lift its cumulative gross to $61.3 million. Directed by Shen Chunyang and written by Ma Duo, the satirical feature stars real-life comedic pair Shen Chunyang and Xiao Shenyang alongside Jia Bing and Yu Yang as an uninspired middle-aged couple forced to navigate marital strain after swapping bodies.

	Mainland China’s overall weekend box office contracted to $16.4 million amid an ongoing fall lull. The 2026 year-to-date box office reached $4.75 billion, trailing the same period in 2025 by 29%.

schema.headline: China Box Office: ‘Traces of Justice’ Reclaims Top Spot as Local Debuts ‘Embers’ and ‘The Coffin Swap’ Arrive

title: Nicholas Denton, Hugh Bonneville and Tim Downie Board Elevated Folk Horror ‘Tragedy Man: The Making of Michael Reeves’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Nicholas Denton (“Talamasca: The Secret Order,” “Dangerous Liaisons”) is attached to portray cult British horror filmmaker Michael Reeves opposite
body:
Nicholas Denton (“Talamasca: The Secret Order,” “Dangerous Liaisons”) is attached to portray cult British horror filmmaker Michael Reeves opposite Tim Downie (“Baldur’s Gate 3,” “Outlander”) as Hollywood horror legend Vincent Price in “Tragedy Man: The Making of Michael Reeves.” Hugh Bonneville (“Downton Abbey,” “Paddington”) joins as British producer and distributor Tony Tenser.

	The elevated folk horror feature explores the turbulent relationship between Reeves and Price during the making of “Witchfinder General,” a collaboration that would produce one of Price’s most acclaimed performances and Reeves’ final film before his death at just 25.
	

	U.K.-based Sceadwe Films and CrossBorder Films have teamed to produce the project. Production is expected to begin in late November. CrossBorder Films will handle international sales and introduce the film to buyers at the American Film Market in Los Angeles.

	Sceadwe Films is the U.K. genre production banner co-founded by producer and writer Justin Stanley, while CrossBorder Films is a London-based film production and sales company.

	Set against 1960s London and the haunted countryside of East Anglia, “Tragedy Man” follows the young Reeves as he stakes his burgeoning career on “Witchfinder General.” His financiers bring in Hollywood horror star Price for the lead role, a casting choice Reeves vehemently opposes, seeing the veteran actor’s theatrical style as everything he wants to leave behind. Price, meanwhile, is confronting his own fears of becoming obsolete as Hollywood changes around him.
	

	VFX supervisor Michael Ellis (the “Enola Holmes” films, “Cloverfield,” “The Bourne Legacy”) is attached to make his feature debut as director. The film is based on an unpublished short story by Richard Sheppard, a writer and film historian specializing in horror cinema. Sheppard co-wrote the screenplay adaptation with Stanley.

	Stanley’s previous writing credits include co-writing Lionsgate thriller “Black Butterfly,” as well as projects for Universal Pictures, New Regency, Marc Platt Productions, Fox Television and HBO.

schema.headline: Nicholas Denton, Hugh Bonneville and Tim Downie Board Elevated Folk Horror ‘Tragedy Man: The Making of Michael Reeves’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: John Oliver Dunks on Midterms Losers Elon Musk and Haley Stevens
description: After issuing an urgent warning prior to the midterms about the GOP’s increasingly troubling ties to neo-Nazis (with a little dig at Elizabeth Holm
body:
After issuing an urgent warning prior to the midterms about the GOP’s increasingly troubling ties to neo-Nazis (with a little dig at Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans, of “You Can See Everything” infamy, thrown in for good measure), John Oliver returned to the “Last Week Tonight” desk on Sunday to bask in the Democrats’ blue tsunami that saw them wrest back control of Congress in imposing fashion.

	“It has been a busy week and, given the midterm results, a pretty good week, too!” Oliver exclaimed at the top of his HBO show. “Democrats won so big on Tuesday it was sometimes genuinely hard to take all the positive results in.”
	

	Oliver opined how it was “genuinely hard to believe Texas had just turned blue,” adding it was “hard to process” all the wins, including 22 state trifectas, Chris Pappas becoming the first openly-gay man elected to U.S. Senate, Deb Haaland of New Mexico being the first Native American woman elected governor of a U.S. state, and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms elected the first Black woman governor of a U.S. state.

	The comic also applauded how, “Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan, meaning all the hateful shit thrown his way did not work, and also that this woman [Haley Stevens] imploded her own political career for nothing. Then, you realize Susan Collins lost too! A decade of having to listen to her express reservations about something before going ahead and doing it anyway are finally fucking over.”

	But wait, there’s more: “Then it hits you that Elon Musk wasted so much money! The half a billion dollars he spent to try and buy the election just went up in flames faster than a parked Cybertruck. Speaking of which: we also learned this week he’s ending production of Cybertrucks, which isn’t an election result but kind of feels like one.”
	

	Yes, Musk spent nearly $500 million during the midterm election cycle, including $200 million to (unsuccessfully) defeat Senator-elect James Talarico in Texas; while Stevens, a supposed Democrat, backed GOP candidate Mike Rogers over her primary rival (and eventual winner) El-Sayed.

schema.headline: John Oliver Dunks on Midterms Losers Elon Musk and Haley Stevens

title: Donald Trump Says He Was ‘Kidding’ About Making Dana White His Press Secretary
description: President Donald Trump has said he was only kidding about appointing Ultimate Fighting Championship president and CEO Dana White as his next White
body:
President Donald Trump has said he was only kidding about appointing Ultimate Fighting Championship president and CEO Dana White as his next White House press secretary.

	Following the ousting of Katie Zacharia from the role, Trump wrote on Truth Social Saturday: “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”


	On Sunday, however, Trump said it was “just a little fun,” according to AP.
	

	“I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump said, speaking to the media in Florida before leaving for Washington D.C. White is due to visit Trump at the White House on Monday.

	As Variety reported Saturday, it was always unclear just how serious Trump was about offering the job to the executive, but the speculation was the latest in recent news regarding potential press secretaries. Trump had been asked during an interview whether musician Nikki Minaj would be considered for the position, to which he responded: “That’s a good idea. I think I’ll have to think about that… I’m going to think about that.”

	Zacharia served as Trump’s press secretary for just five days before she was let go — the shortest tenure in White House history. She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who held the position from Jan. 20, 2025 through Aug. 27. In October, she announced she joining Fox News Channel as a contributor. At 27, she was the youngest person in American history to hold the position.

schema.headline: Donald Trump Says He Was ‘Kidding’ About Making Dana White His Press Secretary

title: Tate McRae and Doechii Choreographer Robbie Blue Among World Choreography Award Winners
description: Robbie Blue, the choreographer for pop and rap stars Tate McRae and Doechii, took home three World Choreography Awards at the 2026 ceremony. He and
body:
Robbie Blue, the choreographer for pop and rap stars Tate McRae and Doechii, took home three World Choreography Awards at the 2026 ceremony. He and his associates were recognized for the intricate moves of McRae’s “Saturday Night Live” dance and Doechii’s electric 67th Grammys performance.

	The 16th annual ceremony took place Nov. 8 at the Avalon Hollywood, honoring choreographers across the globe for their innovative work over the year. Kevin Stea, who has a long career in the arts choreographing Michael Jackson, Prince, Gloria Estefan, Lady Gaga, Beyoncé and more, returned to host. The event featured live performances from Chucky Klapow, Becca Sweitzer, Kevin Stea, Marie Poppins, Holden Maples, Erica Klein and Kelly Sweeney.
	

	“This is an extraordinary one-night-only celebration bringing the world’s most exceptional dance talent together on one stage,” Allen Walls, the WCA founder and producer, said.

	There are eight categories of awards: Motion Picture, Music Video, Television Reality/Variety Show, Television Award Show/Special, Television Episodic, Commercials, Digital Content and Digital Content Independent.

	Among the winners are “Dancing With the Stars” pro Mark Ballas for his 2025 freestyle dance with “Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” Whitney Leavitt to Frank Sinatra’s “My Way” and Shay Latukolan for Jungle’s “Keep Me Satisfied” music video. Blue and his associates were also recognized for the choreography in the viral Gap ad featuring Katseye to “Milkshake” by Kelis.

	Vincent Paterson, a fellow choreographer of Michael Jackson and Madonna, was honored with the Legacy Award.
	

	Read the full list of winners below.

	MOTION PICTURE

	Christopher Scott, Associates Eddie Torres Jr., Danielle Sten Guillermo — “Kiss Of The Spider Woman,” “Gimme Love”

	DIGITAL CONTENT

	Mark Ballas — “My Way”

	TELEVISION AWARD SHOW / SPECIAL

	Robbie Blue, Associate Ashley Kole — 67th Grammys, Doechii

	DIGITAL CONTENT INDEPENDENT

	Sergio Reis — “Bittersuite”

	TELEVISION EPISODIC

	Brooke Lipton — “Palm Royale”

	COMMERCIALS

	Robbie Blue, Associates Lucas DeBiasi, Marie Spieldenner — Gap, Better In Denim

	MUSIC VIDEO

	Shay Latukolan — Jungle, “Keep Me Satisfied”

	TELEVISION REALITY / VARIETY SHOW

	Robbie Blue, Associate Bailey Holt — Saturday Night Live, Tate McRae

title: ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Dazzling Cast Can’t Elevate the Musical’s Muted Narrative
description: One of the most beautiful things about legends and myths is they often stem from the truth. Written by playwright and lyricist Angelica Chéri and d
body:
One of the most beautiful things about legends and myths is they often stem from the truth. Written by playwright and lyricist Angelica Chéri and directed by Stevie Walker-Webb, the new Broadway musical “Wanted” is inspired by Chéri’s great-great aunts, Mary (Solea Pfeiffer) and Martha Clarke (Liisi LaFontaine). These Black women living in post-emancipation Texas decided to pass for white and wield their beauty and guns to save their family’s land and legacy. Unfortunately, despite the exceptional performances and vocal talent, the play’s actual narrative isn’t as compelling as it could be.
	

	According to the Kinfolk, the ensemble that leads the audience into the story, this tale begins in 1893 in Marlon, Texas, in the middle of a cotton field. After struggling and saving with their mother, Tallulah (a phenomenal Ledisi), sharecroppers Mary and Martha are eager to finally buy the land the Clarke family has worked on for generations. However, the landowner, Mr. Billingsley (Nathan Quay Thomas), has other plans. Fueled by racist fury when the women offer a sum of $200 for ownership of the property, he snaps. Rejecting their hard-earned money, he claims the Clarkes are behind on rent and demands double, or he’ll evict them.

	With little recourse beyond their pale skin, courtesy of their long-vanished French father, Mary and Martha set out together beyond Marlon’s country roads to earn money and save themselves and their mother from destitution. Yet as single women traipsing around the 19th-century American South, they become an immediate target. Armed with Ole Bessie, Tallulah’s pistol, the sisters soon discover that stealing and intimidation earn them cash much faster than any other profession. Though their criminality affords them more than they ever hoped, their carefully laid plans are thwarted when they stumble upon a saloon owned by the infamous Jesse Banks (Bradley Jaden), who immediately sets his sights on Mary.
	

	Yet the Clarke sisters aren’t really the outlaws the play tried to make them out to be. Aside from a couple of stick-ups and some seducing and scheming, the rebel storyline fizzles before it even really gets started. Instead, Mary finds herself enamored with Jesse, a wealthy white man who has no idea she is a Black woman. Meanwhile, Martha reluctantly finds herself charmed by Elijah (Luke James), a Black man employed by Jesse. Only through their relationships with these different men does the conflict between the sisters arise, making the story less intriguing and more par for the course.

	Though the narrative isn’t particularly distinct, especially since the central plot largely focuses on the sisters finding love rather than their outlaw status or the true costs of passing, the show’s vocal talent is beyond exceptional. Ledisi, LaFontaine and Pfeiffer are all phenomenal. Backed by an orchestra led by Paul Byssainthe, Jr., the play has several standout numbers, including “Inheritance” and “Mary’s Nightmare.” But the rest of the musical numbers and lyrics don’t exactly pack a punch. Scenic design by Beowulf Boritt and video and projection design by Stefania Bulbarella give the stage much-needed depth, allowing the audience to understand the texture of the time period and place. The singing itself, though, is truly the glue that holds the entire show together. 

	Though passing as an act of defiance and self-preservation is certainly interesting, these themes have been explored to a fault in films like 1934 and 1959’s “Imitation of Life” and books like Brit Bennett’s “The Vanishing Half” and Nella Larsen’s “Passing.” Unfortunately, what Mary experiences isn’t a new or refreshing take on the subject. Instead, “Wanted” presents her as dangerously naive and bewilderingly selfish, far from the badass criminal she’s initially depicted as.

	In the end, because of its overstuffed book and themes, “Wanted” doesn’t quite know what it’s about, resulting in an underwhelming account of who the Clarke sisters were and why their story stands out in American history. Lacking true focus and direction, and leaning heavily on a rushed love story, “Wanted” works best as a musical album. As a Broadway show, however, it simply doesn’t measure up.

schema.headline: ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Dazzling Cast Can’t Elevate the Musical’s Muted Narrative

title: Goldwyn Bets on French WW2 Epic ‘De Gaulle’ Crossing Over to U.S. Audiences: ‘It’s the Story of an Ally’
description: Antonin Baudry’s two-part World War II epic about Charles de Gaulle made its U.S. premiere Saturday at the American French Film Festival in Los Ang
body:
Antonin Baudry’s two-part World War II epic about Charles de Gaulle made its U.S. premiere Saturday at the American French Film Festival in Los Angeles, drawing a seven-minute standing ovation after both installments, each running more than two and a half hours, played back-to-back to packed audiences at the DGA Theater.

	The €74 million production, starring Simon Abkarian as the French general and Simon Russell Beale as Winston Churchill, marks one of Pathé’s boldest gambles following “The Count of Monte Cristo” and the two-part “The Three Musketeers,” which were also distributed in the U.S. by Samuel Goldwyn Films.
	

	After a slow start in France, the films quietly gained momentum through word of mouth, becoming a domestic box office success and selling over six million tickets, and are now gaining traction internationally. In the U.K., the first installment, “De Gaulle: Resistance,” which charts De Gaulle’s heroic battle to build a Resistance movement after France surrendered to Nazi Germany in 1940, currently ranks as the highest-grossing French-language film of the year. “De Gaulle” has also just been acquired in China – a rare feat — where Light Films will release it in late November.

	In the U.S., Goldwyn is rolling out the epic theatrically across major U.S. markets, including New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Washington, D.C., Seattle, Austin, Minneapolis, Houston and Atlanta, while making it available nationwide on transactional VOD. The second film, “De Gaulle: Liberty” will be released in early December.

	Speaking to Variety during the American French Film Festival, Peter Goldwyn said he’s betting that the sprawling saga can appeal to U.S. audiences even if it revolves around a French historical figure that many aren’t familiar with.
	

	“The films have proven themselves, and audiences are audiences, whether they’re American or French,” Goldwyn said. “It’s an amazing feat of filmmaking that you don’t quite see anymore and ultimately, World War II is an easy entry point for U.S. audiences.”

	“U.S. audiences have been very much enthusiastic consistently about stories about Roosevelt, about Churchill, and I think that the story of De Gaulle is relatively untold in America,” he continued, adding that the “staggering scope and scale of what (De Gaulle) accomplished as one man is pretty amazing.”

	Goldwyn argued that the films’ cinematic ambition places them closer to Hollywood blockbusters than conventional European arthouse fare.

	“As a film itself, you’re looking at something on the scale of ‘The Odyssey.’ It’s just really broad and massive, and yet instead of getting lost in the effects and the war itself, it really does come down to a character study which drives the story along. So you’re not just sitting there watching World War II play out,” he said.

	“The only thing that makes it an arthouse movie is because it’s in a foreign language,” he added, pointing out that the French language “makes it hard for theaters to commit on that wide of a screen count.”

	As such, Goldwyn opted to pair the theatrical run with a nationwide transactional VOD release, giving the films the best chance of finding their audience. 

	“In France it had this sort of slow start and was really discovered, but theaters in the U.S. don’t have the patience or time to let things be discovered. It’s sort of you’re in and you’re out,” he said. “So it’s a combination method.”

	The distributor is mounting a single campaign for both installments, targeting not only arthouse moviegoers but also history buffs, schools, cultural institutions and younger audiences through social media. “I think it’s enhancement, especially when you have two movies of this length, you need word of mouth and if you can only have a couple showtimes a day, you can only get so many people into the theaters,” Goldwyn said.

	The appeal of the films also lies in the fact that they challenge the familiar American and British narratives of World War II, exposing the tensions between De Gaulle, Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt, played by Campbell Scott.
	

	Baudry and his co-screenwriter, Bérénice Vila, read more than 150 books and dug into historical archives to reconstruct the general’s extraordinary journey from an isolated, virtually unknown military officer in 1940 to the leader of the French Resistance, as well as his relationship with Churchill and Roosevelt.

	“They had different conceptions of war. Roosevelt, for his part, thought Churchill was being completely absurd with his romantic ideas about supporting this admirable little leader called De Gaulle. To Roosevelt, the idea of Free France was a little fantasy of Churchill’s,” said Baudry.

	The director said the complicated relationship among the three leaders remains largely unknown outside academic circles.

	“All of this history has never really been told. Historians, real historians who research this period and have access to the sources, know all of this, but the general public doesn’t. And the version of history taught in schools is not very complete,” he said.

	Despite the historical complexity, Baudry wanted the films to be accessible to viewers with no knowledge of De Gaulle, so he organized early screenings for young students outside academic circles.

	“My goal was that you could watch the film without any outside references, without ever having heard of that period or of De Gaulle,” he said.

	One of Baudry’s boldest choices was casting Abkarian, a renowned actor with a career in film and theater who isn’t a bankable star, to embody the towering historical figure.

	Abkarian spent roughly six months preparing for the role of De Gaulle, whose rigid posture, distinctive voice and almost eccentric behavior have long made him difficult to portray.

	“I read the screenplay more than ten times. I read it and reread it and annotated things,” Abkarian told Variety. “There was nothing to change in the writing, not even a comma. The dialogue was really well written.”

	The iconic monologues came more naturally. “There were the great speeches, and that’s where I feel at home because I come from the theater and I know how to approach them.”

	Abkarian also transcribed every line of his dialogue into a small notebook that he carried throughout the 150-day shoot and eventually gave to Baudry.
	

	“All the dialogue went right up to the very last page. I hadn’t planned it that way, but every page was filled. I didn’t have to use another notebook,” he said.

	But the actor eventually abandoned the idea of simply reproducing De Gaulle’s mannerisms. “You can’t represent a character like this in a strictly anthropological way. You can invoke him, evoke him, but you can’t actually become him. And it wouldn’t make sense to try,” he said.

	One breakthrough came when Abkarian and Baudry spent an evening recording De Gaulle’s speeches together.

	“We explored how far I could go in approaching his voice, its frequency, its musicality and the way he emphasized certain words that wouldn’t naturally occur to you. I had to understand his logic, the way he articulated his thoughts through language,” Abkarian said. “I couldn’t make him speak in the ordinary, conversational way I’m speaking to you now. Between doing nothing and caricature, I had to find the right balance.”

	The screenplay portrays Churchill and De Gaulle as unlikely allies bound by mutual admiration despite their frequent clashes, and Abkarian found an easy partner in Russell Beale.

	“Simon is an incredible actor who has a profound understanding of great texts, and we have the same approach to the craft,” Abkarian said. “The writing provides such rich material for the actors, particularly for De Gaulle and Churchill.”

	For Abkarian, Churchill and De Gaulle were united by an idealism that set them apart from Roosevelt’s political pragmatism.

	“Churchill and De Gaulle were romantics. They recognized that quality in each other. That’s why they developed that friendship,” he said. “And that’s what makes their relationship beautiful, as well as mad and contradictory.”

	Abkarian is less certain than Goldwyn about how Americans will respond to the films’ portrayal of their wartime leadership, but he believes De Gaulle’s defiance could strike a chord, particularly in today’s political climate.

	“There may be something in De Gaulle’s struggle that speaks to Americans’ own battles, to their sense of nobility and their democratic convictions,” he said. “I think that, from that point of view, Americans could recognize themselves in the Gaullist struggle.”
	

	Goldwyn, for his part, sees a hero Americans will recognize. “It’s a story of an ally,” Goldwyn said. “This man was very patriotic, which I think is very American. He didn’t go along with what his government dictated and said, ‘I don’t believe this, I need to fight for my country.’”

schema.headline: Goldwyn Bets on French WW2 Epic ‘De Gaulle’ Crossing Over to U.S. Audiences: ‘It’s the Story of an Ally’

title: Cannes Prize-Winning ‘Brink of Dreams’ Director Ayman El Amir Preps Dark Comedy About Egypt’s Obsession With ‘Fame at All Costs’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Egyptian filmmaker Ayman El Amir, who co-directed the groundbreaking, Cannes prize-winning documentary “The Brink of Dreams,” is developing his nex
body:
Egyptian filmmaker Ayman El Amir, who co-directed the groundbreaking, Cannes prize-winning documentary “The Brink of Dreams,” is developing his next feature, “A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon.” The satirical comedy is among the projects that will be taking part in the Crossroads Co-Production Forum of the Agora, the industry arm of the Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival.

	Set in a remote Egyptian village, the film follows George, a quirky Coptic dreamer who’s desperate to be a famous actor but is stuck playing an extra in low-budget films. As his village is promised a sewage mega-project, George also catches a miraculous break on a space-themed reality TV show promising a voyage to the moon. Overnight, he becomes a celebrated national hero.
	

	But when the show is exposed as a scam, George becomes a laughingstock. Returning home in disgrace and exiled by his community, he discovers the village’s promised project was also an illusion. The failed star embarks on a journey of self-discovery, uncovering his true identity, finding a profound sense of belonging and reclaiming a defiant spirit.

	“A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon” is written and directed by El Amir and produced by Nada Riyadh for their Cairo-based shingle Felucca Films. The duo co-directed “The Brink of Dreams,” which won the Golden Eye Award for best documentary at the Cannes Film Festival in 2024 — the first Egyptian film ever to be honored with that prize. The pair was also named Variety MENA Talent of the Year.

	Speaking to Variety in Thessaloniki, El Amir explains how his film explores a precarious moment in Egyptian history, a period of “unregulated capitalism” where the government’s lavish visions of a “New Republic” have given way to “new satellite cities, massive highways, grandiose bridges, extravagant beach resorts and new upmarket luxurious gated cities” — an unattainable reality for the millions of ordinary people living on the margins of this ambitious “Egyptian Dream.” 
	

	The film, says the director, asks the question: “How do you plan a future that is not in your control?”

	“In a society where we only discuss failure as a precursor to success, ‘A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon’ is a contemporary dark comedy fable that satirizes our obsession with success and fame at all costs,” El Amir says.

	“At its core, this film explores the boundaries of aspiration in contemporary Egyptian society, the invisible barriers that block out dreams of equality, opportunity and self-made success. It’s a deeply reflective story about identity, belonging and how we perceive ourselves,” he continues. “Yet beneath those layers, it’s about the sudden, jarring realization of stepping out from under a predetermined gaze and finally being witnessed as you truly are.”

	“The Brink of Dreams” was a coming-of-age story that followed the Panorama Barsha Troupe, an all-female theater group in a remote village in southern Egypt who take to the streets to act out their plays denouncing underage marriage, domestic violence and patriarchy in a deeply conservative society.



	

					Ayman El Amir and Nada Riyadh co-directed “The Brink of Dreams.”
									Courtesy Ahmed Ismail Mousa
	



	With “A Pair of Shoes,” El Amir returns to Barsha, where he spent several years while making his previous film. There, he says, the punishing realities of daily life — “an unforgiving sun, a parched earth and a high unemployment rate and a failed economy” — stand in stark contrast to the glitzy narrative of a “New Egypt.”

	It is this “unexplored and unseen” version of Egypt that he wants to bring to the screen.

	“One of the important motivations for me to embark on this new project is what I experienced upon the theatrical distribution of ‘The Brink of Dreams,’” he explains. During audience Q&As for what was the first Egyptian documentary ever to be distributed commercially in the country, El Amir was “surprised by the stereotypes the audience” — city-dwellers from Cairo and Alexandria — “have about their fellow citizens who live in the south.

	“During the last decade, Egyptian cinema became predominated by images of people living in luxury compounds and gated communities that represents only less than 10% of Egyptian society,” he says. “We rarely see people from the south on screen. For me, that is a question of representation that I find very important and urgent.”
	

	“A Pair of Shoes in the Dark Corner of the Moon” is in advanced development, with initial financing in place and plans to shoot at the end of 2028. The project was recently awarded at the CineGouna Industry Platform, where it received a $10,000 grant from Arab Radio & Television and a $10,000 production grant from ESLSCA University.

	“Our primary goal at Thessaloniki is to connect with strategic European and international co-producers who share our vision and can help us navigate funding, financing and European co-production avenues,” says El Amir. He notes that while the film’s village scenes will be shot on location in the south of Egypt, “the space-themed reality TV show sequence can be shot in any other co-production countries.”

	The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

title: Anthony Chen-Produced ‘Somewhere in the South’ Wins Top Prize at Taiwan Creative Content Fest Pitching Awards, ‘Reunion Dinner’ Takes Three
description: “Somewhere in the South,” a Malaysian feature written and directed by Tan Ce Ding and produced by Anthony Chen, the Singaporean director of Cannes
body:
“Somewhere in the South,” a Malaysian feature written and directed by Tan Ce Ding and produced by Anthony Chen, the Singaporean director of Cannes Caméra d’Or winner “Ilo Ilo,” won the $35,000 TAICCA × CNC Feature Film Grand Award at the 2026 Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) pitching awards in Taipei.

	The project is produced by Giraffe Pictures, the Singapore-based company co-founded by Chen, and Evil Genius Studio. The prize is backed by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA), which organizes TCCF, and France’s National Center for Cinema (CNC). The other Grand Award winners were series “Saga,” from BiZ Productions and Elephant Story; Eddy Cinéma’s animated project “Wilderness of the Greenriver”; and Singing Cicadas’ documentary “A Day’s Worth.”
	

	Set in a forgotten town in southern Malaysia, “Somewhere in the South” follows 25-year-old Boon, who helps his mother run their struggling temple. When a by-election brings his charismatic childhood friend JC back to town to lead a campaign, Boon is hired as JC’s driver and reluctantly becomes the party’s tiger mascot. Then the mascot is stolen, and his fragile sense of identity is thrown into question.

	“Reunion Dinner,” from Make A Deal International Production, led the awards with three wins: the Videoland Ingenuity Award, MPA Asia Pacific Grand Award and the award from NAFF, the Network of Asian Fantastic Films project market at South Korea’s Bucheon festival.

	Several other projects received two awards each. “Saving Tuvalu,” produced by Media Stockade and Filmtank, won the Hakka Public Communication Foundation Confluence Award and Taiwan Mobile: Content Power Award. Critical Hits Production’s “Turns Out It’s Not BL But BFF” received the 2026 TCCF MyPick Project Award and Kaohsiung Film Archive’s KFA Original Award. Mirror Entertainment’s “Romance in Hell” won the Hami Video Creativity Award and udnFunLife IP Potential Award.
	

	In the series category, Model Universe’s “Sunlight Delivery” received the Blintn Next Hit Award and EBC Original IP Potential Award. Seika Works’ “The 16th Night Kitchen” won the Mediacorp Award and TVBS Storytelling Impact Grand Award. In the documentary category, “Parachute Kids,” from Walking Iris Media and Your Sister Films, received both the Doc Edge Award and Mega Bank C&E Foundation Best ESG Award.

	Mirror Fiction’s “The Three Witches of Shetou” won both the TAICCA Award: Best Story and friDay Video Original Story Award. In her remarks, Mirror Fiction sales director Sharleen Liu thanked author Chen Si-hong for creating the story.

	“On the surface, it is absurd and funny, but underneath it explores loss and pain, asking how we keep living after losing so much. Even when life feels as absurd as a disaster, we can still live with gusto. We hope this distinctive Taiwanese story can reach audiences around the world,” Liu said.

	TAICCA chair Sue Wang said that this year, the agency saw progress among the pitching teams and their projects were resonating more strongly internationally. “They are ready to pursue co-productions with international partners, and both Taiwanese and overseas teams are approaching these collaborations with a strong sense of ambition,” Wang said.

	Wang added that animation pitches showed a clearer, more precise vision for IP and a broader sense of how it could develop. “For documentaries, TAICCA hopes to develop more tailored support. Cultural ESG [environmental, social and governance] can be a good entry point, and we are seeing writers and pitching teams think more commercially,” she said.

	This year’s TCCF Pitching slate featured 92 project and story pitches across film, series, animation, documentaries, publishing and comics. Industry participants from 28 countries attended. The wider TCCF program included 107 Market exhibitors from seven countries and territories. Its four-day Forum held 12 sessions with more than 20 speakers discussing international co-production, streaming-platform consolidation, IP, short-form content and AI.

title: Kaia Gerber Shares Post About Grief After Brother Presley's Death
description:
Kaia Gerber
                          Grief Comes in Waves ...
                          After Pr
body:
Kaia Gerber
                          Grief Comes in Waves ...
                          After Presley's Death
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kaia Gerber is sharing a heartfelt message about coping with grief after her brother Presley's death at 27.
      
    
            Taking to Instagram ... she shared a stack of various books and novels that dealt with the topic of grief before picking out a particularly poignant quote by Joan Didion.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Kaia shared ... "Grief, when it comes, is nothing we expect it to be. Grief has no distance. Grief comes in waves, paroxysms, sudden apprehensions that weaken the knees and blind the eyes and obliterate darkness."
      

            Just three weeks ago ... Kaia spoke out about Presley's death, sharing a lengthy letter addressed to him with her Instagram followers.
      
    
            Kaia admitted she was "quite literally, down on my f***ing knees" ... and said she was "born loving you" and would "die loving you."
      
    
            As you know ... Presley was discovered unresponsive in his room at Santa Monica rehab facility on Sept. 20. He had just checked into the facility hours prior.
      
    
            While police investigate his death as a suspected overdose, his official cause of death is still pending.

Chris Brown
                          Baby Mama Wants His Bank Records
                          In Effort to Get $30K a Month Child Support
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 9, 2026
                            1:00 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Chris Brown’s baby mama is working overtime to see the singer’s finances in her bid to collect a bigger child support check … claiming she’s been roadblocked for months by his team ...  TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Diamond Brown, the mother of Chris’ daughter Lovely, and Chris’ business managers appear to be at a standstill over the records being produced.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Diamond says she needs to see them as part of her attempt to collect more child support through a case she brought against Chris. She says the singer has an estimated net worth of $50 million … but is only paying her around $7K a month … which she thinks should be much higher.
      

            As part of her battle, Diamond revealed she subpoenaed Chris’ business managers … asking to see Chris’ finances … but they objected.
      
    
            Diamond said it’s hard for her to figure out his true income … and needs to see his records to get an accurate idea of what he makes and what he can afford to pay in child support. She said she only has $10K to her name and believes Chris should pay at least $30K per month in child support.
      
    
            As we previously reported, Chris’ other baby mamas called Diamond out publicly following her move in court. They claimed Chris is a good dad who takes care of his children.

title: Egypt Train Crash Leaves At Least 7 Killed and Over 100 Injured
description:
Egypt Train Collision
                          At Least 7 Killed, Over 100 Injured
body:
Egypt Train Collision
                          At Least 7 Killed, Over 100 Injured
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Two trains collided in Egypt, resulting in the deaths of at least seven people and leaving over 100 injured.
      
    
            The crash went down 30 miles south of Cairo in the al-Ayyat district ... AP News reported.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The train traveling to the Fayoum province slammed into the rear of a train heading to Aswan ... resulting in a derailment.
      

            Following the wreck ... those injured were transported to nearby hospitals after emergency crews and a crane were dispatched to the area.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi wrote on X ... "I have directed state agencies to provide the necessary medical care, promptly investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."
      
    
            This latest crash comes just weeks after two high-speed trains collided in Spain, resulting in 69 deaths and more than 100 injured.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Admits Affair, Company Probing Alleged Chinese Recruitment Plot, Report
description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
                          Admits Affair, Company Probes Alleged Spy Plot
body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
                          Admits Affair, Company Probes Alleged Spy Plot
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Nvidia's married CEO Jensen Huang has openly admitted to an affair, leading to a probe by his company into an alleged foreign recruitment plot ... according to a bombshell report.
      
    
            Jensen -- who is married to Lori Huang -- made the startling admission to employees in an internal message obtained by the Financial Times.
      
    
            The exec apparently wrote ... "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
      

            While he didn't name the person he had an affair with ... the Financial Times reported that top US officials claimed Jensen had a romantic relationship with a woman named Alice Huang that U.S. intelligence believed was a Chinese spy.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Both the Financial Times and New York Times cite Alice as the person listed in a classified memo alleging she was a possible recruit of the Chinese Ministry of State Security.
      
    
            Alice is an exec at Megaspeed -- which did business with Nvidia. Before his apology ... Jensen told Bloomberg News in October that his interactions with her were "related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual."
      
    
            Following Jensen's internal message about the affair ... Nvidia's board said they would begin an independent probe "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
      
    
            The board added in their statement ... "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information."
      
    
            We've reached out to Megaspeed AI for comment on Alice's behalf ... so far, no word back.
